classification_signals: The introduction explicitly states the book's purpose is to 'survey the new models currently being put forth in the sciences and humanities concerning our human natures, with particular relevance to architecture' (p. 21) and to consider 'new scientific and humanistic models in architectural terms' (p. 2). It outlines a 'main premise' (p. 23) and discusses implications for design, rather than presenting new empirical data. The book is structured as a series of essays exploring these theoretical connections.
title: Architecture and Embodiment: The Implications of the New Sciences and Humanities for Design

findings.antecedent: Reciprocal interaction between environments and human cognitive abilities/outlooks
findings.consequent: Relevance of traditional 'nature versus nurture' arguments
findings.quote: Traditional arguments such as "nature versus nurture" are rapidly disappearing because of the realization that just as we are affecting our environments, so too do these altered environments restructure our cognitive abilities and outlooks.

findings.antecedent: Biological and technological breakthroughs
findings.consequent: Quality of built environments
findings.quote: these same discoveries also have the potential to improve in significant ways the quality of our built environments.

findings.antecedent: Rhythmic exercises (eurhythmics) tapping into the body's natural rhythm
findings.consequent: Harmonization of body with neural activities and enhanced working efficiency of the creative mind
findings.quote: Dalcroze viewed music not as an end in itself but rather as a means for individuals to expand their happiness and creativity—that is, as a way to harmonize the body with the neural activities of the brain and to bring about a "co-ordination between the mind which conceives, the brain which orders, the nerve which transmits and the muscle which executes."

findings.antecedent: Body's movements, postures, homeostasis, and emotional responses
findings.consequent: Influence on thinking processes
findings.quote: we are now beginning to appreciate the role that the body's movements, postures, homeostasis, and emotional responses play in all of our thinking processes.

findings.antecedent: Environmental fields of stimuli
findings.consequent: Sculpting and re-engineering of biological systems, leading to continual self-reconstitution
findings.quote: For we are beginning to see the extent to which we, as evolved biological organisms, are continually reconstituting ourselves within environmental fields of stimuli that are sculpting or re-engineering our biological systems with ever quicker speeds and with multiple layers of depth and complexity.

findings.antecedent: New models in sciences and humanities
findings.consequent: Relevance of the Cartesian distinction between matter (res extensa) and thought (res cognitans)
findings.quote: The famous Cartesian distinction between matter (res extensa) and thought (res cognitans), which ruled science and philosophy for much of three centuries, is the most obvious casualty.

findings.antecedent: Body and emotional underpinnings (at conscious and preconscious levels)
findings.consequent: Shaping of how we think about and actively engage the world
findings.quote: our body and its emotional underpinnings, at all conscious and preconscious levels, shape how we think about or actively engage the world

findings.antecedent: Built environment (fashioned by architect or planner)
findings.consequent: Location where body and emotional underpinnings shape thought and engagement in urban cultures
findings.quote: and in our urban cultures this shaping generally takes place in the built environment that the architect or planner fashions.

findings.antecedent: Organism moving within the environmental field (exteroception through proprioception)
findings.consequent: Active visual perception, co-perception of the self, and extraction of invariants or patterns
findings.quote: visual perception as the engagement of the whole organism moving within the environmental field—that is, exteroception through proprioception. From such a perspective, the organism and the environment are complementary and reciprocal in their connectedness, and perception is an active extracting of invariants or patterns that always involves the co-perception of the self.

findings.antecedent: Cultural environment
findings.consequent: Separation from the natural environment
findings.quote: one in which the cultural environment cannot be separated from the natural environment, 'as if there were a world of mental products distinct from the world of material products.'

findings.antecedent: Genetic sequencing and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
findings.consequent: Critical rethinking of many cherished premises of human behavior
findings.quote: Genetic sequencing and such innovative technologies as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which allowed us for the first time to peer inside the working brain, have more or less forced us to rethink critically many of the most cherished premises of our behavior.

findings.antecedent: Advancing technologies (e.g., web dependence) and expansive models of embodiment
findings.consequent: Relevance of older social-science models (e.g., nature vs. nurture)
findings.quote: The meaning of such distinctions is being rapidly eroded and vigorously challenged today by the 'intellectual scaffolds' of our advancing technologies, on the one hand... and by the more expansive models of embodiment, on the other.

findings.antecedent: Environmental conditions
findings.consequent: Alteration of neural connections (brain plasticity)
findings.quote: One factor certainly challenging traditional views of culture is our new under- standing of neural plasticity, or the ability of the brain to alter its neural connections in response to environmental conditions.

findings.antecedent: Technological artifacts of environmental fields (e.g., digital tools)
findings.consequent: Radical change in how we perceive or even think about things over a generation
findings.quote: the technological artifacts of our environmental fields, through their impact on our cognitive structures, can radically change the way we perceive or even think about things over the course of a generation.

findings.antecedent: Historical architectural theory (Renaissance, industrial age, early modernism)
findings.consequent: Ocular bias and exclusive focus on form (objectification of a building)
findings.quote: For many years now we have viewed design with an ocular bias and with an almost exclusive focus on form—that is, with the objectification of a building as a structured composition of formal elements conceived according to a design.

findings.antecedent: Premise that people would align their biological 'blank slates' with cultural artifacts of new formalism
findings.consequent: Delusion, leading to a 'perpetual crisis' in theory
findings.quote: the underlying premise—that people would eventually align their biological 'blank slates' with the cultural artifacts of the new formalism—proved to be a delusion, leading to what Manfredo Tafuri once referred to as the perpetual 'crisis' in theory.

findings.antecedent: New models of how we engage our built world
findings.consequent: Redirection of design focus back to occupants and how they perceive, feel, respond to, and enjoy the architectural experience
findings.quote: the new models of how we engage our built world propose the alternative strategy of returning the focus of design back to those to whom architecture has historically directed its efforts—the occupants of our constructed environments and how they perceive, feel, respond to, and (on seemingly rare occasions) enjoy the experience.

findings.antecedent: Environmental stimuli
findings.consequent: Preconscious emotional responses (somatic, visceral, electrical, and chemical events) that precede conscious awareness of feelings
findings.quote: Emotions are somatic, visceral, electrical, and chemical events ('gut feelings') whose neurological footprints can be captured with neuroimaging technologies. By most definitions, they precede our conscious awareness of feelings—that is, they precognitively inform our response to things.

findings.antecedent: Emotional circuits
findings.consequent: Integration with the neural maps of reason
findings.quote: Emotional circuits, in fact, are but a part of the very same neural maps by which that inhibiting factor of reason (a late-comer to the evolutionary game) operates.

findings.antecedent: Multisensory, neurologically interconnected architectural experience
findings.consequent: Deep embedding of emotions, initially coding whether an environment is pleasing or not
findings.quote: And because we respond to the environment through multiple corporeal senses, neurologically interconnected, emotions are deeply embedded in every architectural experience from the start. They initially code whether an environment is pleasing or not, regardless of whether it appears within a traditional or avant-garde dressing.

findings.antecedent: Perceptual stimuli
findings.consequent: Mental simulation or embodiment (via systemic firing of specialized neurons)
findings.quote: This systemic firing of specialized neurons means that we mentally simulate or embody most of what we apprehend through the senses, whether we are aware of it or not.

findings.antecedent: Mirror neuron activation (embodied simulation)
findings.consequent: Ability to animate the inanimate physical environment
findings.quote: we animate the inanimate physical environment with which we come into contact.

findings.antecedent: Mirror neurons
findings.consequent: Connection with our environment and means to apprehend and form relationships with physical surroundings
findings.quote: Mirror neurons, in this sense, connect us with our environment; or rather, they provide us with the means by which we apprehend and form a relationship with our physical surroundings.

findings.antecedent: Aspects of a building
findings.consequent: Internal simulation in a pre-reflective manner
findings.quote: In explaining how we internally simulate aspects of a building in a multisensory and emotional way, they also suggest that we do so largely in a pre-reflective manner

findings.antecedent: Artistic play and its connection with social rituals and ceremonies
findings.consequent: Evolutionary basis
findings.quote: The last of the essays considers the new issues that anthropology and ethology are currently delineating—specifically the evolutionary basis for artistic play and its connection with social rituals and ceremonies.

findings.antecedent: Origin of art residing in social relations and making things 'special' through dexterity and care-inspired participation in communal events
findings.consequent: Architect's persona shifts from object-creator to participant in social relations
findings.quote: For if the origin of art seems to reside in social relations and the way in which we make something 'special' through our dexterity and care-inspired participation in these communal events, then the artistically minded architect might perhaps assume a different persona than someone simply creating a self-satisfying 'object' of design.

findings.antecedent: Algorithmic possibilities and technological ambitions
findings.consequent: Architectural creativity
findings.quote: Otherwise, architectural creativity tends to be subdued or overtaken by algorithmic possibilities and technological ambitions

findings.antecedent: Current scanning technologies (confining subjects to a motionless condition)
findings.consequent: Ability to fully capture multisensory, three-dimensional architectural experience
findings.quote: our multisensory, three-dimensional experience of the built environment cannot be so captured with current scanning technologies, which presently confine one to a motionless condition within a lab.

findings.antecedent: Perceptual studies of materials, colors, textures, and forms
findings.consequent: Relevance to design
findings.quote: The perceptual studies of materials, colors, textures, and forms, for instance, have direct relevance to design.

findings.antecedent: Research on the proprioceptive talents of dancers
findings.consequent: Translation into the architectural experience of space
findings.quote: research with regard to the proprioceptive talents of dancers, for instance, can be translated into the architectural experience of space.

limitations: Current scanning technologies confine study to motionless conditions, limiting the capture of multisensory, three-dimensional architectural experience (p. 28).
Architects have been reluctant to participate in these discussions due to humanities being pushed out of curricula by intensifying technological and professional demands (p. 28).
Ivory-towered design studios remain uncritically saddled with conventional axioms regarding the objectification of form (p. 28).
The profession at large seems content to practice 'the pure aesthetics of a bygone brand of speculation' (p. 28).
minimum_safe_summary: This book introduces a theoretical framework for understanding architecture through the lens of new scientific and humanistic models, particularly focusing on embodiment. It argues that recent discoveries in biology, neuroscience, psychology, and anthropology challenge traditional dualistic views of mind and body, revealing how our embodied nature, emotions, and environmental interactions profoundly shape our perception and cognition of the built world. Key findings include the interconnectedness of mind, body, and environment, the role of emotions and mirror neurons in architectural experience, and the impact of neural plasticity and technology on human perception. The author highlights limitations in current architectural theory and research methods, such as the objectification of form and the inability of current neuroimaging to capture dynamic, multisensory experiences.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Cognition is fundamentally shaped by the body's interactions with its environment.
The environment provides opportunities for action (affordances) that are directly perceived by an embodied agent.
Human experience is fundamentally subjective and situated in the lived body and world.
